"Below are questions proposed for a research problem, each with the reframing behind it. Classify each one.
kind: \"reframe\" if it changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before; \"copies\" if it only runs the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side; \"other\" otherwise.
meets_criterion: \"yes\" or \"no\" for this criterion: none given; answer NA
Give for each a quote from the proposal and a reason of at most 25 words. Decide only from the text below; do not use tools.
Problem:
**ml-ensemble-extremes · Ensemble size for rare extremes in a machine-learned weather ensemble.** seed pick · compute tested: yes · plan expects: the lever · PASS

**Question.** Does 10 to 1,000 AIFS-ENS members beat 50 for top-percentile wind, temperature, and rain probability forecasts, or does shared model error cap the skill?

**What is known.** HENS Part 2: 7,424 SFNO members per day for 92 summer-2023 dates; showed huge ensembles sample 4-sigma tails and reduce outliers. Whether AIFS-ENS, whose members are exchangeable draws of one afCRPS-trained distribution, keeps gaining skill past 50 members or saturates from shared model error.

**Hypothesis.** More members keep helping: 1,000 members sample top-percentile tails far better than 50, so extreme-event scores keep improving [s_hens].

**If compute is the lever.** Skill on top-percentile wind, temperature, and rain keeps rising past 50 members: 1,000 members sharpen the tails and improve extreme-event scores.

**If not.** Skill flattens near 50 members: members are exchangeable draws of one trained distribution, so shared model error caps tail sharpness and extra members add nothing.

**Test.** Run 7,000 fifteen-day AIFS-ENS v1 forecasts (7 dates x 1,000 members) on eight A100 40 GB GPUs; subsample 10-1,000 members, score top-percentile wind/temperature/rain probabilities against ERA5 with fair CRPS and Brier scores, and test whether skill still rises past 50 members.

*Compute axis.* Ensemble members per forecast: 10–1,000 members, 6 levels. Closest prior: 7,424 [s_hens], not beyond it.

*Restructuring.* none.

**Check first.** Reproduce the published 4-minute N320 member time and 38 GB memory; one control run must match ECMWF open data within ensemble spread [s_crps_paper]. Tolerance: timing within +/-25% of 4 min; 38 GB memory fits; control field within the ensemble's own member-to-member spread at each lead time (GPUs are non-deterministic, so exact reproduction is not expected).

**Would not show.** Applies to AIFS-ENS v1 medium-range extremes on 7 dates; not a multi-season reforecast, other models, subseasonal leads, or direct proof that shared error causes any saturation.

*Cost.* Plans $963.17 of the $1,000 budget over 74.3 machine-hours, leaving $36.83. Main guess: peak filesystem usage [g], measured after $19.90 of spend; the budget is reached if it is 15× higher. Full scale: A 30-date multi-season reforecast at 1,000 members, $3,980, 3.98× the budget.
Proposals: [{\"index\":1,\"bottleneck\":\"Skill differences between member counts are averaged over only 7 held-fixed verification dates; across-date variance dominates the standard error of the skill-vs-N slope, so members past roughly 50-100 per date buy precision on a quantity that stays swamped by date noise. Extra members purchase more of the same.\",\"assumption\":\"That members per forecast is the compute axis that limits the answer, with the 7 verification dates held fixed.\",\"reframe\":\"Treat the run budget as an experimental-design problem: estimate the variance components (across-date vs within-date sampling) and reallocate a fixed number of member-forecasts across (dates x members) to minimize the standard error of the slope of skill vs log N, rather than maximizing members on few dates.\",\"question\":\"For a fixed budget of 3,000 member-forecasts, which (dates x members) allocation - 7x400, 15x200, or 30x100 - gives the smallest standard error on the slope of top-1% fair-Brier skill vs log2 N, measured against ERA5?\",\"measure\":\"Pilot: run 2 new dates at 200 members plus reuse the 50-member control (about 400 new runs, roughly $55, about 4 machine-hours). Estimate across-date and sampling variance of the Brier score at N=50 and N=200, then solve the analytic optimal-allocation formula for the fixed budget.\",\"compute_after\":\"The full budget buys the optimal split (likely around 30 dates x 100 members, roughly $413): extra compute then buys independent verification dates, i.e. new information, instead of redundant draws from one distribution.\",\"exact\":\"Standard error of the fitted slope of fair-Brier skill vs log2(members) for top-1% wind, temperature, and rain exceedance probabilities verified against ERA5.\",\"expected\":\"Across-date variance dominates at N>=50, so the optimal allocation shifts compute toward dates and the slope's standard error drops by roughly a factor of 2 at equal dollar cost.\",\"fails_if\":\"Within-date sampling variance still dominates at N=200, meaning large member counts genuinely add measurable skill and the original 1,000-member design stands.\",\"closest_prior\":\"HENS Part 2 [s_hens] ran 92 dates x 7,424 members but never reported the variance components or an optimal (dates x members) split; the afCRPS paper [s_crps_paper] used a fixed 51-member operational set.\"},{\"index\":2,\"bottleneck\":\"Members are exchangeable draws of one afCRPS-trained distribution, so the N-dependence of any threshold-probability score is binomial sampling noise with a known 1/N form; running 1,000 members mostly measures arithmetic and cannot move the N-infinity cap set by model error.\",\"assumption\":\"That the saturation point and the asymptotic skill must be found empirically by actually running the large ensembles.\",\"reframe\":\"Change what is measured: fit the score's a + b/N law from nested subsamples of a few hundred members and extrapolate the N-infinity asymptote directly, instead of buying the curve point by point with full-fidelity members.\",\"question\":\"From a + b/N fits to fair-CRPS and fair-Brier on nested subsamples of 10-200 members over the 7 dates, is the extrapolated N-infinity skill for top-1% wind/temperature/rain probabilities statistically distinguishable from the N=50 skill (difference greater than 0.02 Brier)?\",\"measure\":\"Run 7 dates x 200 members (1,400 runs, roughly $193, about 15 machine-hours), or first test the 1/N law for free on the published 51-member ECMWF open-data control (about $0). Bootstrap subsample 10-200 members and fit per variable.\",\"compute_after\":\"If the asymptote is flat, the question is answered with about 5x less member compute, and the saved budget redirects to more dates or perturbed-model diversity; only a failed 1/N fit justifies the 1,000-member runs.\",\"exact\":\"Extrapolated N-infinity fair-Brier and fair-CRPS (the a parameter of the a + b/N fit) for top-1% wind/temperature/rain exceedance probabilities, with bootstrap confidence intervals.\",\"expected\":\"The 1/N law fits within bootstrap error and the asymptote lies within about 0.01 Brier of the N=50 value, demonstrating saturation from 200 members instead of 1,000.\",\"fails_if\":\"Scores deviate systematically from a + b/N (for example in the far tail, where member exchangeability could break down), meaning large-N runs carry real information and must be executed.\",\"closest_prior\":\"HENS [s_hens] demonstrated 4-sigma tail sampling at 7,424 members but did not test whether skill follows the exchangeable-draw a + b/N asymptote; standard Monte Carlo theory predicts it must if members are exchangeable.\"},{\"index\":3,\"bottleneck\":\"The fixed 7-dates x 6-member-levels factorial commits all 7,000 runs before any data are examined; compute is spent even where the answer is already decided, while the real objective is binary - does skill keep rising past 50 members, yes or no - not the full curve.\",\"assumption\":\"That the experiment needs a fixed design at six member levels, fully executed before analysis begins.\",\"reframe\":\"Change the objective to the yes/no decision and reorder the work: a group-sequential test that adds members in batches of 50 and stops as soon as the confidence interval on the skill gain versus the 50-member baseline excludes the decision threshold in either direction.\",\"question\":\"With a group-sequential test at tolerance 0.02 Brier on the paired difference from the 50-member baseline, after how many members per date does the question 'skill keeps rising past 50 members' resolve on the first 2 dates, measured on top-1% wind/temperature/rain Brier skill against ERA5?\",\"measure\":\"Run 2 dates in batches of 50 members up to 400 (at most 800 runs, roughly $110, about 8.5 machine-hours; expected $30-55 with early stopping), applying the sequential test after each batch.\",\"compute_after\":\"Compute becomes adaptive, spent only until the decision resolves; if 'no gain' resolves at 100-200 members, the remaining roughly $850 buys more dates or a perturbed-checkpoint diversity test instead of redundant members.\",\"exact\":\"Stopping member-count and the accepted hypothesis of the group-sequential test on the paired difference in top-1% fair-Brier skill between N members and the 50-member baseline.\",\"expected\":\"The test accepts 'no gain past 50' by 100-200 members per date, cutting member compute 5-10x relative to the 1,000-member plan.\",\"fails_if\":\"The true gain sits near the 0.02-Brier tolerance, so the test rarely stops early and costs about the same as the fixed design.\",\"closest_prior\":\"Group-sequential designs are standard in clinical trials; neither HENS [s_hens] nor the AIFS-ENS evaluation [s_crps_paper] used adaptive stopping, fixing member counts in advance.\"}]
